title: What Advice Would You Give Yourself
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article warns leaders against answering questions and advice requests too quickly, arguing that instant answers rob team members of the chance to develop their own judgment. It recommends a specific redirect question, "What advice would you give yourself?", as a way to pause the exchange and invite the other person to reason through the issue first. The author notes this doesn't derail the conversation or signal unwillingness to help; instead it signals that the leader won't always be available and that self-generated insight matters. It closes by naming several companion questions that accomplish the same slowing-down effect while giving the leader more context before responding.
points: Answering questions immediately denies team members the chance to develop their own insight and judgment over time.
The question "What advice would you give yourself?" pauses the exchange without signaling unwillingness to help.
In many cases, the advice a person gives themselves matches what the leader would have said, reinforcing both parties' confidence.
Companion questions like "What has worked in the past?" and "What have you seen others do?" achieve the same slowing effect.
quotes: Leaders held in the highest regard field questions about more private matters, including counsel about family, careers, and relationships.
But responding to this inquiry too quickly has a significant downside.

After fielding an inquiry or request for feedback, good leaders start the conversation with a simple but effective question that asks the other party to think through the issue on their own: What advice would you give yourself?
Interestingly, in many cases, the advice they would give themselves is exactly what the leader would offer, further cementing their confidence and insight.
Leaders develop people. They won’t always be there to guide them.
